In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and may God bless our Prophet Muhammad and his family and all his Companions and grant them peace. We had reached …

Then he returned to Mecca and attached himself to Abu Bakr al-Humaydi, and transmitted from the companions of Tawus, the companions of Mujahid and the companions of ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah. Then he went to Medina with a letter from the governor of Mecca to Malik — the governor of Mecca being his cousin, of the descendants of al-Saʾib ibn Yazid. When he came to him, Malik paid the letter no regard at all and said: Since when has learning needed intercessions? But before long Malik came to know al-Shafiʿi's intelligence and the excellence of his mind, and so brought him near and drew him close and shared his wealth with him — to the point that Malik would hold the sandal and hand him the sandal; and al-Shafiʿi had been poor before that. In his first period in Medina he did not confine himself to Malik's circle: rather, when Malik rose from his circle, al-Shafiʿi would go to other circles. Malik had chairs set before him for those of his students who were close to him, and he assigned one of these chairs to al-Shafiʿi. In Malik's session people would take dictation by way of three repeaters: one repeater would rise when Malik's voice ended, or when the voice of the one reading to him ended, and raise his voice; and a repeater would rise when that man's voice ended; and another repeater would rise when that man's voice ended, in the circle.

At that time they used to say: It is among the adornments of this world that a man should say, "Malik informed us." Al-Shafiʿi came to Malik having memorised the Muwaṭṭaʾ before he came to him, and attached himself to him in that period. And those chairs — their occupants had a standing in Medina: those who sat on the chairs before Malik had a standing in Medina. That is why, when Malik became angry with ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, ʿAbd al-Malik swore for a year that he would not sit for a year upon the chair; so he abandoned Malik's circle for a year, and the chair remained unoccupied for a year. A man came and wanted to sit on it, and Malik said to him: Are you not ashamed to sit on a chair from which ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun rose only yesterday? So that chair was left unoccupied for a year, waiting for ʿAbd al-Malik, until he returned to it.

When he went to Iraq he studied under Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani and took the fiqh of Abu Hanifah from him. And a number of the leading figures of the people of Iraq studied under him, such as Abu Thawr and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Shafiʿi, who also became known by the name al-Shafiʿi; and it was from him that the two of them transmitted his old school. The old school of al-Shafiʿi was transmitted only by Abu Thawr and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Shafiʿi in Iraq. Then he travelled to Egypt and settled there and lodged with ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam, the companion of Malik, and lived in his house and died in it. Al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, lived fifty-four years.

Then from al-Muzani's time onwards, composition within the school began. Among the earliest of those who composed within the school was also Abu Jaʿfar al-Tahawi, who has been mentioned before, in the Hanafi school; and his maternal uncle al-Muzani. He was at first a Shafiʿi, and a disagreement arose between him and his uncle when he composed a book on the school of al-Shafiʿi and contradicted in it some of al-Muzani's transmissions. So al-Muzani swore that he would never be fit for learning — he swore that his sister's son would never be fit for learning. So he went off to Iraq and took the school of Abu Hanifah, until he composed his book Mukhtaṣar al-Ṭaḥāwī in the Hanafi school. When he completed it he said: God have mercy on my uncle; if he were alive he would have to expiate his oath. And al-Tahawi's books have been mentioned before.

Then there appeared in the school some of the leading figures who are "possessors of positions", such as al-Asamm, Abu Saʿid al-Istakhri and Ibn Kajj; and these dispersed through the various regions.

The book al-Umm is considered among the most important books of the Shafiʿi school, and al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar composed upon it Talkhīṣ al-Ḥabīr for the documentation of the hadiths of al-Rafiʿi the elder — the documentation of the hadiths of Fatḥ al-ʿAzīz. And al-Bayumi composed upon it his book al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr fī Gharīb Lughat al-Rāfiʿī al-Kabīr, which is one of the important lexicons of the language, especially in that it gives attention to morphology, the inflection of verbs and their patterns. For this reason it is the jurists' lexicon, the one relied upon in fiqh; its name is al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr fī Gharīb Lughat al-Rāfiʿī al-Kabīr. All these books are printed. Fatḥ al-ʿAzīz was printed long ago as far as the hajj only, together with al-Majmūʿ — the old printings of al-Majmūʿ — and it was not completed until last year, when it was printed complete. As for Talkhīṣ al-Ḥabīr, it has been printed in several editions, one of them with documentation in the margins, and that is the best of them; and it was printed in another edition together with al-Majmūʿ, and in separate editions. And al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr likewise has been printed in a number of editions, the best of them the old Bulaq edition, then later editions, and the latest of them the Dar Lubnan edition — this one which the Christians print. They print lexicons, and from these they deliberately delete certain entries: the entry n-k-ḥ they drop from every lexicon they print. They dropped it deliberately from al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr and from Mukhtār al-Ṣiḥāḥ and from al-Muʿtamad and from a number of the lexicons they have printed — and I do not know the reason for it. They drop this entry in particular: between n-k-th and n-k-d, the entry n-k-ḥ; and they delete this entry in its entirety.

Then came the Imam al-Nawawi, who was the master of the school without dispute and is the renewer in the view of the Shafiʿis; he is like Ibn Qudamah among the Hanbalis.

Then his book Minhāj al-Ṭālibīn, which is an abridgement upon which God set acceptance, and which in the Shafiʿi school is like the Risālah of Ibn Abi Zayd among the Malikis. It even resembles the Risālah in its arrangement and its division into chapters: Ibn Abi Zayd usually opens each chapter with a verse or a hadith upon which the chapter turns, and then mentions the rulings after it. Likewise al-Nawawi in the Minhāj says: The Book of Sale — "and God has permitted sale and forbidden usurious gain (ribā)" — and so on: he opens every chapter with a verse or a hadith connected with it. This book is one upon which God set acceptance, so its commentaries and glosses and annotations became many and it became the school's point of reference. Whoever studies the Shafiʿi school, or teaches it, or researches in it, the first book his eye falls upon in this school is the Minhāj. Among the most important commentaries on the Minhāj are Mughnī al-Muḥtāj by al-Sharbini and Tuḥfat al-Muḥtāj by al-Ramli — al-Ramli was given the title "the little Shafiʿi" for the excellence of his mind and his intelligence — and Bahjat al-Muḥtāj by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami. Upon these there are many glosses, such as the glosses of al-Shirwani and the gloss of al-Qalyubi and the gloss of ʿUmayrah; all of these are printed. And some glosses were composed upon certain chapters only, such as Ṣawb al-Rukām, which is a gloss on the Book of the Judiciary alone; its author is ʿUbayd Allah al-Saqqaf, one of the sayyids of Yemen, of Hadramawt, and one of its great scholars. He knew the Minhāj and its commentaries by heart, and whoever reads this book of his knows his mastery in learning; and that is why one of the poets praises him in an ode in which he says:

*The universe stands still at the counting of their qualities* … among al-Nawawi's books, for example, are some that serve the books of those before him, such as his book on the rare words of the language of al-Tanbīh. And al-Tanbīh too is an abridgement in the Shafiʿi school, by the Sultan of the Scholars, al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam. Al-Tanbīh is printed, and the commentary on the rare words of al-Tanbīh is also printed, by al-Nawawi.

Then his famous book Tahdhīb al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Lughāt, which is considered among the useful lexicons in the field of fiqh, because it gives the technical terms of the Shafiʿi school and explains what is rare in the language of the jurists, and gives biographical notices of those who are mentioned in the Shafiʿi school. In general it is a very precise book, resembled by the book of the judge ʿIyad which has been mentioned before, namely Mashāriq al-Anwār. Al-Nawawi has many other books in which he gathered much of the sayings of the leading Shafiʿi scholars — and for all that he lived only forty-three years. He stayed studying at the House of Hadith in Damascus for eleven years, in which he never slept lying down: when he wanted to sleep he would lean against one of its pillars and sit with his knees drawn up, so that he slept sitting, lest sleep get the better of him.

He was among the ascetics and devoted worshippers, and that appeared in his compositions, so that God set upon them a wondrous acceptance and blessing. There is no house among the houses of the Muslims in which there is a book, after the Book of God, but that there is in it a book of al-Nawawi's — either Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn, or al-Adhkār, or his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, or any other of his books. His supplications were answered, and he was a man of scrupulousness who kept clear even of some of the lawful, because it entailed a certain immersion in the appetites: for the whole period of his stay in Damascus he did not eat cucumber, because it leads to the opening of the appetite. Likewise, among the important books for the coverage of the school's derived rulings are the abridgements of Zakariyya al-Ansari, the ḥāfiẓ and student of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar. He has two abridgements in the Shafiʿi school, and God set acceptance upon them too, so that people received them with acceptance, and many commentaries were composed upon them, such as the book Manhaj al-Ṭullāb; and he has another book named Itḥāf al-Ṭullāb.

These are the most important printed books which are the point of reference to which recourse is had in the details of the school.

Then after this we come to the Hanbali school. Al-Shafiʿi says, on the occasion of a visit of his to the Imam Ahmad:

*They said: Ahmad visits you, and you visit him. If he visits me it is out of his own excellence, and if I visit him it is out of his excellence.*

And Ahmad answered him with the words:

*If you visit us, it is out of an excellence in you that you bestow on us; may we be deprived of neither of the two states from you, nor …*

Al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, used to come in Iraq to the companions of Yahya ibn Saʿid al-Qattan, such as Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Maʿin and ʿAli ibn al-Madini, and would say to them: You are the pharmacists and we are the physicians. So he would present his hadith to them, and they would discuss its hidden defects with him and those narrators whom they impugned. If al-Shafiʿi did not have a good opinion of the narrator, or knew him better than they did, he would abandon transmitting from him; and if al-Shafiʿi had a good opinion of him, or knew him better than they did, he would not name him explicitly in the transmission. That is why al-Shafiʿi often says: "from the one who is trustworthy in my view" — when they had discussed him with him and their opinion of him was poor while he knew him better, or his own opinion of him was good.

The Imam Ahmad transmitted the Muwaṭṭaʾ of Malik, from Malik, through eighteen of Malik's companions. Among these are al-Shafiʿi, Qutaybah ibn Saʿid, ʿAbd Allah ibn Maslamah al-Qaʿnabi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Yusuf al-Tinnisi, Yahya ibn Yahya, Abu Musʿab al-Zuhri, Suwayd ibn Saʿid and Ismaʿil ibn Abi Uways: Ahmad transmitted the Muwaṭṭaʾ from all of them and presented it to all of them. That was because he did not meet Malik, and he used to wish that he had met him, and said: Since Malik was denied to us, God compensated us with Sufyan. So he was eager to hear from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, because he was of that generation to which Malik belonged.

*And by the sound and the weak they meant to hold us back from our judgement upon a chain in which a people plunged, and it was said: Malik is his patron; and choose where it is traced back through him* — because Ibn al-Salah mentioned only that the best of chains is al-Shafiʿi from Malik from Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace; for al-Bukhari said: the soundest chain for the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, is Malik from Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar. So Ibn al-Salah added and said: al-Shafiʿi from Malik. Then al-ʿIraqi added Ahmad and said: Ahmad from al-Shafiʿi, from Malik from Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. Yet Ahmad transmitted only a few hadiths in the Musnad by this chain, by way of al-Shafiʿi — even though he transmitted the whole Muwaṭṭaʾ from him, and in it are all the hadiths of Nafiʿ, all of them hadiths of Malik by way of Nafiʿ. So by this chain there are approximately five hadiths in the Musnad: the hadith of Ahmad from al-Shafiʿi from Malik from Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar.

As for following the historical sequence of the compositions in this way, no one has given attention to it; and even in the Hanbali school what is mentioned is not a connected chain, and what we too have mentioned here is not a connected chain. What is intended by it is only what lights the way for the researcher and the teacher of this discipline: the books that are within his reach and in his hands. Either these books are famous and in circulation among people, like the printed books in circulation; or else they are a point of reference for researchers which cannot be dispensed with, among the manuscripts that are not lost and destroyed. This is what I choose here in this sequence.

There is no doubt that those who compose works on the generations of the schools, and likewise those who compose works on the biographies of the leading scholars, mention some of the famous books of the school, and likewise give attention to the biographies of their authors. As for the fame of the memorisers of hadith within the Shafiʿi school, its cause is that many of those who gave attention to the memorisation of hadith were the easterners, who were in the lands to which the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, pointed when he said: If this learning were suspended from the Pleiades, men from the kin of this man would reach it — and he pointed to Salman the Persian. So the lands beyond the river, and the lands of Nishapur and Khurasan and Bukhara and others, are the ones in which the memorisation of hadith became famous at the end of the second century of the Hijrah, and throughout the third century and the fourth — about two and a half centuries in which the memorisation of hadith became famous in this region, settled in it, and was the object of scholarly travel; and the Shafiʿi school was prevalent in many of its areas.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj was more or less upon the school of Malik, the Baghdad school; and Abu Dawud was upon the school of Ahmad. So memorisation is not particular to one school rather than another; only, this is what became famous. Among the great ḥāfiẓs of the Shafiʿis, Abu Hatim ibn Hibban al-Busti became famous, and likewise Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Hakim, and likewise Abu Bakr al-Bayhaqi, and others besides these among the great memorisers — and even among the later ones, such as al-ʿIraqi, al-Mizzi, al-Haythami and al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, and Zakariyya al-Ansari and al-Sakhawi and al-Dhahabi and Ibn Kathir and the companions of Ibn Hajar, such as al-Daymi and al-Sakhawi and Zakariyya al-Ansari, and then their students after them, such as al-Suyuti.

As for the spread of the Shafiʿi school, what actually lay behind it was the presence of certain judges and governors upon this school in various regions, and especially in Syria and Iraq. Among the great Shafiʿi judges, the Imam al-Mawardi became famous, whom they title "the most judicial of judges", and likewise Ibn Abi al-Dam al-Hamawi, the judge of Hamah. And so that was a cause of the school's spread to a certain extent.

As for the Hanbali school, it is the last of these schools to appear, because its leading figure came later in age, and because of the afflictions he was met with at the beginning of his fame and of the gathering of the students of learning around him; and also because he was renowned for hadith, so that people occupied his time with hadith rather than with independent reasoning on legal questions. For all that, this school is considered the broadest of the schools from the standpoint of independent reasoning, because there is no view in any one of the schools but that the Imam Ahmad has a transmitted report agreeing with it; and then he adds to that some further transmissions peculiar to himself. If a state had been founded upon this school, it would have been the school most fit to spread, because of the breadth of its transmitted reports: a person cannot get outside it. He can act upon any one of the schools and then say: this is my school, the Hanbali school. And for all that, the Imam Ahmad himself wrote nothing in fiqh; he wrote hadith only, and was averse to writing legal questions down. Even so, some questions were recorded from him: his son Salih recorded his questions from him, and his son ʿAbd Allah recorded his questions from him — though Salih's questions are more juristic and ʿAbd Allah's more hadith-based. Abu Dawud recorded his questions from him, and these in fact are more hadith-based. Ibn Haniʾ recorded his questions, and al-Kawsaj his questions, and Ibrahim al-Harbi his questions, and al-Baghawi the younger his questions; and these are the books of questions that became well known among the Hanbalis. Al-Khallal gathered them in his books, and in fact al-Khallal is the one who sifted the school: from him the Hanbali school set out, and by way of his students it became famous. Among his students is his servant ʿAbd al-ʿAziz Abu Bakr, who became known as Ghulam al-Khallal, and likewise al-Barbahari. Then there appeared in it some eminent figures who occupied themselves with many sciences, so that they had a firm footing in learning in various fields — such as Ibn ʿAqil, who left no science without composing on it, and whose book al-Funūn is said to be among the most extensive of books, being four hundred and sixty volumes; and likewise his companions, such as al-Tamimi and Ibn Hamid. Then after these came the judge Abu Yaʿla, who became famous for the excellence of his mind and his intelligence, and composed a number of books serving the school, and gave attention to the transmitted reports from the Imam Ahmad, gathering the two views and the two positions: everything in which there are two views, or two positions in the school, or two transmitted reports, he gathered all of it. For all that, it is said that he is in the Hanbali school like al-Lakhmi in the Maliki school; for much of what is ascribed to the school of transmitted reports consists rather of extracted reports, and is not transmitted from the Imam Ahmad's own words. That is why the later scholars object to this: al-Shirazi, one of the leading Shafiʿis in legal theory, discusses the ascription of extracted views to the leading scholars and whether it is permissible to ascribe them to them or not; and likewise Ibn Qudamah. Even so, many of the views ascribed to the Imam Ahmad are extracted from his statement, and sometimes they contradict his explicit statement: he gives an opinion on a question with a ruling concerning which no report to the contrary is known from him, but he gives an opinion on a question resembling it with a contrary ruling, and so Abu Yaʿla extracts for him a report contradicting the first report in each of the two questions. He extracts for it a derived case with a report agreeing with the legal opinion in the first question; and in the first there is likewise a report agreeing with the ruling in the second question. So he makes two reports in each of the two questions. These are called "the extracted reports" among the Hanbalis. In general, the settled position of the Hanbalis is that it is permissible to ascribe the extracted reports to the leading scholar: they are ascribed to him and counted among his statements.

Among the eminent figures who appeared in this school is al-Tufi, who is one of the masters of legal theory. But he had great extravagances in the creedal field and in his independent reasonings and in many matters in which he departed from the main road — such as his criticism of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. When he read the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī — Ibn ʿAbbas used to say: Thursday, and what a Thursday! The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, called for something on it and said: Bring me writing materials; I shall write for you a document after which you will not go astray. Then the clamour grew about him and ʿUmar said: The Book of God suffices us. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Leave me; it is not fitting that there should be dispute in the presence of a prophet — and so he did not write that document for them. At this al-Tufi became angry with ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and made the whole matter out to be a problem that came from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.

Likewise he holds that benefit takes precedence over the text — that benefit (maṣlaḥah) is given precedence over the explicit text (naṣṣ) without qualification; and this is among the matters that are not to be understood. He is one of the later scholars, roughly among the students of Ibn Qudamah.

Among them likewise is Abu al-Khattab Mahfuz al-Kalwadhani, who also gave attention to gathering the transmitted reports of the school. But in fact the learning of the Hanbalis passed to Muwaffaq al-Millah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi. This learning had been in his household before, and among the Maqdisis generally; for many of the people of Jerusalem were among the scholars of the Hanbalis. The settling of the Hanbali school in Jerusalem and in Nablus in former times is well known, and it is related that the Hanbali masters in Nablus were blind. A scholar of the Hanafis came to them wanting to spread the Hanafi school in Nablus in Syria; they debated him and he defeated them, so they combined against him. And the Maqdisis, when the Crusaders occupied Jerusalem, went out from it to Damascus and settled in a suburb of it called al-Salihiyyah. There Ibn Qudamah, may God have mercy on him, built a strong fortress for his household, for the house of Qudamah, and built houses for them in it. He was famous for good management and soundness of judgement and firm arrangement in the affairs of religion and of this world; and his household did not know that he was building a building for them until it was complete, and then he brought them out to it and settled them in it.

This used to happen among the noble houses of Syria: they would build fortresses and build palaces within them in which they gathered — as happened with Shayzar, which was a fortress belonging to the house of Munqidh; indeed they had a governorship and a princedom in it, until God afflicted them with the eart[hquake] …

Ibn Qudamah, may God have mercy on him, composed a large number of books in the school and arranged them upon the ways of a scholarly curriculum: such as the book al-ʿUmdah, which is composed for young boys; then above it the book al-Muqniʿ, which has only two transmitted reports and does not go beyond them; then above it the book al-Kāfī, which is broader than it; then above that al-Mughnī. People gave the book al-Muqniʿ very great attention, so that it was in fact the book of the school; and for this reason the commentaries upon it and the abridgements derived from it became many. Among its commentaries is al-Mubdiʿ bi-Sharḥ al-Muqniʿ by Ibn Muflih the younger, who is the grandson of Ibn Muflih the elder, the student of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah. Among them likewise is al-Sharḥ al-Kabīr, which is in fact the siftings of al-Mughnī. For Ibn Qudamah composed al-Mughnī as a commentary on the Mukhtaṣar of al-Khiraqi, and al-Khiraqi had abridged in his Mukhtaṣar the books of al-Khallal, but it was not tightly made, nor divided into chapters in a way conforming to what is known in Hanbali arrangement, and its questions were jumbled. For this reason he says: the Mukhtaṣar of al-Khiraqi could not bear the book al-Mughnī. The book al-Mughnī is a commentary on the Mukhtaṣar of al-Khiraqi, but it could not bear it; it is bigger than it. So Abu ʿUmar, who is Ibn Qudamah's nephew, asked his permission to empty out the book al-Mughnī and write it upon al-Muqniʿ, and he gave him permission for that; and so it was named al-Sharḥ al-Kabīr ʿalā al-Muqniʿ. It is in fact the very words of Ibn Qudamah in al-Mughnī, but he arranged them upon al-Muqniʿ and altered nothing in it except rarely. Likewise among the important commentaries on al-Muqniʿ is the book al-Inṣāf by al-Mardawi, in which he attempts to gather the transmitted reports in the school and to make clear which of them is the school's position. He relied on the old books of the Hanbalis, such as al-Muḥarrar by the grandfather Ibn Taymiyyah — ʿAbd al-Salam, the grandfather of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah — and the book al-Riʿāyatayn and the book al-Hidāyah and the book of Ibn ʿAbd al-Hadi, and others of the old books of the Hanbalis. In all of them he gives the conflicting views and the differing transmitted reports from the leading scholar, and the extracted positions — the positions held by the school's own adherents — and gathers them and chooses one view from among them and says: this is the school's position. In that he relies only upon transmission: so if Ibn Taymiyyah began with it in al-Muḥarrar, and Ibn Qudamah declared it sound and adduced evidence for it and said "and in our view", then it is the school's position among the Hanbalis. So he gathers these indications together and extracts from them a single report which is the school's position — that is, the one relied upon in the school. In general this book is among the most important of the Hanbalis' books for establishing what the current position of the school is among them.

Likewise, among the attention given to al-Muqniʿ is that it was also abridged in al-Iqnāʿ; and upon al-Iqnāʿ al-Buhuti composed his comprehensive book named Kashshāf al-Qināʿ ʿan Matn al-Iqnāʿ, which they call "the shovel of the school": it gathers all the derived rulings that have a connection with the school. Its arrangement is good, and its author relies essentially on the preferences of Ibn Qudamah. And among the attention given to al-Muqniʿ likewise is that it was abridged in Zād al-Mustaqniʿ min Matn al-Muqniʿ by al-Hajjawi, upon which Mansur al-Buhuti also composed his book al-Rawḍ al-Murbiʿ bi-Sharḥ al-Zād al-Mustaqniʿ. This book became famous among the later Hanbalis, and upon it are the Najdi glosses: the gloss of al-ʿAnqari and the gloss of Ibn Qasim. The gloss of al-ʿAnqari is in three parts, three volumes, and the gloss of Ibn Qasim in seven.

The gloss of Ibn Qasim is the more important, because it also contains the statements of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and his preferences and the preferences of his students. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said, in praise of Ibn Qudamah: No one more learned in fiqh than he has entered Syria since al-Awzaʿi. That is a great commendation. Then after Ibn Qudamah came a number of jurists, and the school spread on account of Ibn Qudamah's books — until there came the Imam Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Halim ibn ʿAbd al-Salam ibn Taymiyyah, who found no time to compose on the school; but he corrected the Hanbalis' errors in transmission and became a practitioner of independent reasoning in the weighing of views within the school: whatever he held preponderant or chose is the chosen position among the Hanbalis. And although he did not write a book devoted to the derived rulings of the Hanbalis, his students wrote a number of books on that, the most prominent of them being the book al-Furūʿ by Ibn Muflih the elder. In this book he confines the transmitted reports and the derived questions in the school, and then comments on them with his words: "our shaykh said" — meaning by it Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.

This book was relied upon by a number of those who came after him, and many of the later abridgements rely upon it.

These are more or less the most important books of the Hanbalis which the researcher and the teacher of the school needs.

As for the Hanbali school, its spread was at first in Baghdad, and then it was undermined there until the vizier Ibn Hubayrah restored it to it when he took the vizierate; he had a great scholarly standing, and the jurists of his time used to gather around him. And in Syria the school spread only through the work of Ibn Qudamah and then of those who came after him, among the most famous of whom is the Imam Ibn al-Jawzi, who was the finest preacher of Syria without exception.

Then after them came Ibn Taymiyyah and then his students, such as Ibn Rajab and Ibn Muflih and Ibn al-Qayyim: these are the most famous of Ibn Taymiyyah's Hanbali students. The school settled in Syria for a time; it was in Palestine at first, then moved to Damascus and its surroundings. A remnant of it likewise remained in Basra in southern Iraq, and it likewise settled in Najd for periods. As for what some people claim — that the Hanbali school came to Najd only with the call of Shaykh Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhab, when he brought it from Basra — this is not correct. The school was present in Najd; but there were in Najd the other schools as well, and that is why many of those who opposed the Shaykh on the juristic side were adherents of the other schools, such as ….., who was among those who opposed the Shaykh and was Hanafi in school. The school also had a presence in al-Ahsaʾ in former times, before Shaykh Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhab. For all that, there is no doubt that it is among the Shaykh's good deeds that he gave attention to spreading the school in Najd, and especially what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah chose within it.

As for the school, no state was founded upon it before the first Saudi state; and the schools need politics in order to spread, and that is why it did not spread in many other regions. Even so, the presence of some Hanbalis in various places of the world, as individuals, is not to be denied; but they did not have that breadth — in various places in the regions of the world, even in the Maghrib, and even among us, from those influenced chiefly by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and his call, who may have taken up his school.

As for Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah's relation to the school: he did not claim absolute independent reasoning and it was not claimed for him; rather he was a follower of the school of the Imam Ahmad, and he used to state that explicitly, saying: this is the view of our associates, and this is the school's position in our view, and this is what my grandfather chose, and this is what al-Tamimi said, and this is what Ibn ʿAqil said, and this is what Abu Yaʿla and Ibn Qudamah said — and so on; and his statements are brimming with this. But for all that, there is no doubt that he has many preferences, which usually agree with one of the transmitted reports of the school, and may be singular views peculiar to it and set apart from the other schools; so he spreads and champions them, and people therefore oppose him on account of them and claim that he has breached consensus — consensus in their view being the consensus of the four schools only. The fact is that he did not go outside the absolute consensus of the community's practitioners of independent reasoning; rather he was careful not to breach it. He said on one question: if it is not a point of consensus, then my view on it is such-and-such. Ibn al-Qayyim transmitted that from him in the abridgement of Ibn Taymiyyah's preferences, on a question of the waiting period, namely the question of the woman divorced three times observing a waiting period of a single menstruation: he said, if that is not a point of consensus, then I take it. He used to guard himself against questions in which he had not studied whether there was a consensus or not; he was afraid of consensus. So what has become famous about him in the whole world — that he breaches consensus — is not correct. Indeed, I hold that he did not breach even the Hanbali school itself except rarely; but within the transmitted reports of the school, and the school is the broadest of the schools. Even so, he often inclined, for example, to the Maliki school in transactions, and stated his preference for it explicitly — but along with his inclination to it and his preference for it he says: and Ahmad used to take it.

Among the causes of his triumph and of his spread is that the people of his time set upon him with envy and hostility, and that is a cause of the loftiness of his standing. Long ago one of the sages said:

*And when God wishes to spread abroad a virtue that has been folded away, He makes available for it the tongue of an envier.*

Likewise his striving against the Tatars and his standing in their face, and his standing in the face of the oppressive states of his time — God gave him victory by it and left him a tongue of truth among those who came after. Shaykh Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhab likewise did not call for rising against those of the sultans who were astray.

A question about the manner of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah's independent reasoning, and his reliance upon the higher objectives and the benefits, and his gathering of the various texts of the Sharia, and the comprehensive view within them. He says: does he have a counterpart in the other schools?

A question about the reason these schools are ascribed to these leading scholars alone and not to others.

As for the closeness among these schools: there is no doubt that the Maliki, Shafiʿi and Hanbali schools are all one line of descent, namely the school of transmitted practice; and that the Hanafi school is the school of considered opinion, and the Zaydi school is likewise close to the Hanafi school, and the Jaʿfari school is likewise influenced by it. As for the Ibadi school, many of its positions are close to the positions of the Hanbalis. So these are the affinities of the schools. Ibn Qudamah, may God have mercy on him, mentioned that if a Hanbali does not find a legal opinion in accordance with his school — does not find the ruling of the case in his school — to which school should he go? He said: to the school of al-Shafiʿi, because he is the Imam Ahmad's teacher; and if he does not find it, then to the school of Malik; and he should put the school of the Hanafis last. Here is the matter of that line of descent, that line of descent among the schools.

As for partisan fanaticism, it is a phenomenon that does not follow from the school itself; and therefore it cannot be said that one school is more fanatical than another, because it is not a product of the school itself. It rather goes back, as we have mentioned, to environments, and to the feeling of a minority or of one of the schools that others are fanatical against it, or that it is persecuted, or the like; and from this the reaction begins. So too does isolation: if a school is in an environment whose people are ignorant and know no school but this one, they regard it as the religion of God, and everyone who contravenes it as having left the religion — as you know here among the common people: if a person contravenes one of the sunnah acts, or one of the recommended acts (al-mandūbāt), they rise against him as though he had committed one of the reprehensible things, because they have known nothing of the religion but this. Yet the question has various views and schools and evidences, and they know only this one form.

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and I pray for blessing and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and whoever is guided by his guidance and follows his practice until the Day of Judgement. To proceed: the books of the Zahiri school have perished, and nothing of them remains except some of the books of the Imam Ibn Hazm, may God have mercy on him. The most important of them is the book al-Muḥallā bi-l-Āthār, which is an abridgement of his large book al-Mujallā. Most of it was found in draft among his papers and was not transmitted from him, and for that reason some errors occurred in it against the author, may God have mercy on him; and some chapters were lost from it and were then supplied — either his son abridged them from the book al-Mujallā and added them under the heading īṣāl, that is, an addition to what Ibn Hazm wrote, or one of his students did so.

Ibn Hazm treated in his other books many of the investigations within the Zahiri school, the most important of which are his investigations in his book al-Iḥkām fī Uṣūl al-Aḥkām, which is on legal theory, and the small book named al-Nubadh fī al-Uṣūl, and likewise his book on the general and the specific, also in legal theory.

*Though they burn the paper, they will not burn what travels with me wherever my mounts set out.* And there is no doubt that his book al-Mujallā is among the outstanding and beneficial books of the people of learning. But the Spaniards put it in the river when they occupied Cordoba, and so it was among the books that were put in the river and lost. In that deed of theirs many of the very greatest mother-books of Islam were destroyed, and nothing remains of them but a few remnants, which they placed in their library that now exists under the name of El Escorial in Madrid.

As for the Zahiris of the East, their share of fanaticism was greater, because they lived alongside the Hanafis, who possessed state and authority; and for that reason no remnant of their books has survived, even though many of them had a great scholarly standing. Ibn Dawud used to have seventy wearers of the ṭaylasān sitting in his session — that is, seventy scholars attending his lesson. And a very remarkable story happened to him with one of the Sufis. He entered upon him in his session while he was a young man with no beard on his face, teaching, with seventy wearers of the ṭaylasān around him, of the famous scholars, writing from him; and he was on his chair with people around him with heads bowed. The Sufi sat down in his austere garments and heard the lesson and admired it; but he feared self-admiration for its author, and wanted to treat him for it. So when it ended he said to him: Well done, lad; ask about whatever seems good to you. Those around him in the session laughed. And he said to him: I shall ask you only about cupping — intending to mock him, that his dress and his appearance were in the form of a cupper, so that he would only be asked about cupping. The Sufi said: In the name of God; praise belongs to God, and blessing and peace upon the Messenger of God. To proceed: ḥijāmah is of the pattern faʿʿālah from the verbal noun of ḥajama — and he began to speak about its linguistic derivation, then after that about the history of cupping, then about its places on the body, then about the diseases it treats, then about its benefits and its invigoration of the body, then about what has come concerning it in the texts of the Sharia, then about the juristic disagreement over cupping: does it break the fast, and does it nullify ablution or not; and he gave the views of the people of learning and their evidences on the question; then about engaging in it as an occupation and the ruling on that, and "the earnings of the cupper are foul" — the hadith which Abu Dawud brought out — and he gave its hidden defects and what relates to its chain and the biographies of its men. Then he mentioned that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was cupped by Abu Taybah and gave him a ṣāʿ of dates, or two ṣāʿs of dates; and he reconciled the two hadiths with a most excellent reconciliation, upon which people today rely in reconciling the two hadiths. And he brought most remarkable things concerning cupping; then he mentioned what relates to it also in history, concerning the cuppers in Islam and their stories and their famous men; and he mentioned what relates to the instruments of cupping and its lancets; then the disagreement over what is excused of blood between one set of scarifications and another, and what is wiped over of the paper that is placed upon them, and the difference between cupping and the fa[sd, venesection] …

As for the Ibadi school, their reliance in hadith is upon the Musnad of Abu al-Shaʿthaʾ Jabir ibn Zayd, who is among the senior Successors, one of the companions of Ibn ʿAbbas. And their support in fiqh is the book al-Nīl and its commentaries; it is the most important book in their school and has many commentaries. They have books of their own which they write apart from others and hide away in concealed places; they have not been printed to this day. Nothing of their books has come out in print and is sold in the markets except the book al-Nīl and its commentaries. But in Algeria and in Libya and in Tunisia they have manuscript books which they circulate among themselves, and which are given only to whoever has reached a particular standing with them; he is the one who may study those books and have sight of them.

As for the Jaʿfari school, the Imamis have a great number of books, among the most famous of which is the book Sharāʾiʿ al-Islām by al-Hilli. In hadith they rely upon the book al-Kāfī by al-Kulayni and upon some of their transmissions from the books of the earlier scholars; and today they rely upon the compositions of their later scholars. Many of these compositions are in other than Arabic, either in Turkish or in Persian or otherwise, and a number of books of theirs have been printed in Persian and in Turkish. Among their famous references now is the book Taḥrīr al-Wasīlah.

The rapprochement in Iraq between them and some of the people of the Sunnah has led to their having recourse to some of the references of the people of the Sunnah; they have come to rely upon some of them, and especially the books of the later thinkers, and have come to rely upon them. They have books of exegesis which contain the rulings of the Qur'an, among the most famous of which are the exegesis of al-Kashshi and the exegesis of al-Qummi, and others of their exegetes.

As for the Zaydi school, its reliance in origin is on the Musnad of the Imam Zayd; and this Musnad is not the composition of Zayd himself but rather the composition of some of those who gathered his transmissions. Then the leading Zaydi scholars had many books, among which the book al-Azhār became famous: it is the abridgement upon which they depend in the whole of their fiqh. Upon it the Imam al-Shawkani composed his famous book al-Sayl al-Jarrār ʿalā Ḥadāʾiq al-Azhār — so he brought the torrent to sweep away these gardens. The origin of that was that his father was one of their leading scholars and one of their scholars and a judge; and al-Shawkani studied the book al-Azhār under him when he was young. When he reached the obligatory elements of ablution, it mentioned that among the obligatory elements of ablution is washing the two orifices; and the evidence for the obligatory elements of ablution is the words of God Most High: {O you who believe, when you rise for the prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads, and your feet up to the ankles} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:6). So al-Shawkani said: either this is not an obligatory element of ablution, or else it has been dropped from the verse. His father was struck dumb and said: My son, when you grow up you will know the evidence for that. From that time al-Shawkani took an interest in the book al-Azhār, until he composed upon it this torrent that swept it away. And what is noticeable in the Zaydi school is that every one of their authors must produce innovations and departures from the school, so that his book amounts to an independent school and a faction affiliates to it: each faction studies one of their books, affiliates to that book and makes it an independent school. That is why their leading scholars, the leading scholars of the Yemeni state, composed books, and factions arose affiliated to those books — such as the Hadawis, the Mahdawis and the Nasiris, who affiliate to al-Hadi, al-Mahdi and al-Nasir among the leading scholars of the Zaydi state in Yemen.

They composed many books, and especially the leading scholars of the ʿitrah — the kin of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, the People of the House. They have a very great many books on juristic questions, and they have genuinely renewed in them, because their school is a school of independent reasoning and not a school of following a qualified scholar. The Zaydi school is a school that calls to independent reasoning and does not call to following a qualified scholar, unlike many of the schools, even the schools of the people of the Sunnah. That is why, with many of their leading scholars, if you read in their books you find them calling for blatant disagreement with what the Zaydi school holds, in order to follow a hadith which they have declared sound, or which others of the people of learning have declared sound. They do not have the fanaticism that would prevent them from accepting a transmission from others among the people of the Sunnah; and that is why many of their great leading scholars have had recourse to hadiths that are sound in the view of the people of the Sunnah, as against some of their own transmissions — especially since some of them became deeply versed in the science of transmission, so that they came to criticise the transmissions of the Shia and to invalidate them. Among the famous of these is the Imam al-Amir al-Sanʿani, who left their creed entirely — for they hold the creed of the Muʿtazilah — he left their creed and refuted it; and likewise Ibn al-Wazir al-Yamani, who also left their creed and refuted it. The same may be said, and we may classify the Imam al-Shawkani with them, even though he rejects following a qualified scholar in whole and in detail and composed a book on that, and holds that every student of learning, or everyone concerned with learning, must exercise independent reasoning in the religion of God and must not follow anyone — except in transmission only: in comprehension there is no following, whereas in transmission we are compelled to follow. In general, the Zaydi school, on this showing, is hard to describe …

Likewise the books of al-Layth ibn Saʿd were in circulation in Egypt for a time, until al-Shafiʿi settled there; then the books of al-Layth went and no trace of them is known.

Likewise the books of al-Awzaʿi were in circulation in Syria, and especially in Lebanon; then they moved to Andalusia and settled there for a time, and then went entirely — from the coming of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Habib the Maliki. This is about the specialised books composed within a single school. We now come to the comparative books which gather several schools, comparing between them and giving their evidences and discussing them. These books are the ones which a student of learning ought to give attention to studying, after his study of the school in which he grew up or in which he was brought up from the beginning. It is preferable for him to look into the books that relate the higher-level disagreement and discuss the evidences, so that fanaticism may leave him and so that he may know the grounds of the people of learning. It is related from a number of the scholars that they said: no one ought to give legal opinions unless he has four books in his possession. These books have become known as "the four books of the world". These books are: the book al-Muḥallā by Ibn Hazm, which has been mentioned. It treats the higher-level disagreement, and gives the schools of the people of the Sunnah and refutes them and discusses their evidences. Sometimes he succeeds greatly in what concerns the craft of hadith, because of his strength in this field; and sometimes he fails, and especially when he treats the compositions of later scholars which he had not transmitted. For he did not transmit the Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhi; and in his discussion of the prohibition of singing-girls and musical instruments and the position of the majority — he is refuting them — he mentioned the hadiths by which they argue for the prohibition of musical instruments, twenty-one hadiths, and then turned upon them in impugnment, weakening all of them; until he reached one of these hadiths in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi and found no defect for it, and said: Muhammad ibn ʿIsa ibn Sawrah is unknown. Muhammad ibn ʿIsa ibn Sawrah is the Imam al-Tirmidhi, and he is unknown in his view because he did not transmit the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi and had no knowledge of it — whereas we find him, in the other books which he knows by heart, transmitting them with his chains, with the chains of Muhammad ibn Waddah and the chains of Baqiyy ibn Makhlad; for he transmits by these chains the two Ṣaḥīḥs and the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others of the great collections of Islam.

They labour over books with intense labour, and that is why one of the scholars describes them, saying:

*We have companions whose conversation never wearies; they give us the benefit of their learning, the learning of those who have passed away; so there is no trial to be feared and no bad company — and if you were to say they are living, you would not be lying.* And that is why the calamity that befell the Abbasid vizier is well known, when al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi composed for him the book al-ʿAyn and gathered for him in it the language of the Arabs, and he became occupied with it, passing the night memorising it …

This question is about the scholars' attachment to certain great compositions whose existence they wished for. These are very many, and this has been frequent among the scholars; it became well known of a great number of the people of learning that they wished to obtain certain books — indeed …

And this is parallel to what happened to Abu ʿUthman al-Mazini, may God have mercy on him, when a man of the Jews asked him to write out for him the book of Sibawayh for three hundred dinars. He recalled that in the book of Sibawayh there are three hundred Qur'anic verses, and said: I will not put three hundred verses of the Book of God in the hand of a Jew — and he was poor and destitute. While he was in that state, and his daughters were reproaching him over this bargain, the post-horses came asking after him; so he rode the post-horses to the caliph al-Wathiq ibn al-Muʿtasim. He was brought in to him and found that he had a slave-girl who sang, and she recited before him:

And the caliph and his vizier al-Fath ibn Khaqan said to her:

*O our father, may you never depart from us; for indeed, when the lands conceal you* …

He said: And what did you say? He said: I said the words of Jarir:

*Trust in God, who has no partner* . .. He said: Yes, with success, if God wills. And he assigned him three thousand every year. So he told him the story and what had happened, and then al-Fath ibn Khaqan gave him a gift of two thousand, saying: were it not that the caliph gave you three thousand I would have given you that; but out of good manners towards the caliph he reduced it below his gift. Then the caliph gave the slave-girl three thousand, and she presented it to the Shaykh; and so he returned honoured to his family with all these gifts.

Likewise, among their eagerness for books and their attention to them is that a number of those who became famous for conquests and campaigning, such as Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi and others, used to hold sessions for the criticism of new books composed in their time, and books used to be presented to them as gifts. Salah al-Din was not so occupied by striving in God's path and by managing the affairs of states …

*Following upon the praise of the Sovereign, the Bestower — Muhammad and his noble family; and to proceed, the fittest thing to be made clear to them* …

*Al-Nasir, who has divine support; so whoever is other than him, they …*

*And whoever contends with him finds her to be his goal; the beginning is to Salah al-Din; and whoever intends to attain what he wishes, his right hand in it is a helper to the understanding* …

*For kings have taken refuge with him, since there is no escape for them from him.*

*So master this discipline — praiseworthy, important; here I come with it, divided into chapters, summarised, made pure, refined.* Likewise, among the later scholars there is a passion for the books that appear and become famous. Something of this has happened to some of the scholars in this age, so that they used to rejoice over books when they found them, to the point of composing poetry in their joy at them. Shaykh Bab ibn al-Shaykh Sidiyya, may God have mercy on him, when the book al-Muntaqā by al-Baji on the Muwaṭṭaʾ was printed, heard that it had been printed in Turkey and so despatched an envoy from his country, from the land of Shinqit, to Turkey to bring him a copy of it, and went to great expense in that. He says of it in an ode, saying:

I have forgotten its opening; until he says:

*And the jasmine of a garden in the land burst open at the attaining of the book al-Muntaqā* …

Except that … And likewise my grandfather, may God have mercy on him, when al-Taqaṣṣī — which is the stripping down of al-Tamhīd by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr — was printed: one of the ambassadors brought it to him, having been away from the country on a long journey, and he said of it:

*I traced out the traces of praiseworthy deeds, ranging free* … And by God I do not know, even though I am one who knows. And likewise he longed for the existence of a manuscript copy of al-Dhakhīrah by the Imam al-Qarafi.

flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED (house rule 12). Three passages in this tape carry real risk in English. (a) The Sheikh states that Christian publishers in Lebanon deliberately delete the dictionary entry n-k-ḥ from every lexicon they print, naming four titles, and says he does not know the reason. This is an accusation of deliberate religious tampering against an identifiable commercial and confessional group; it is stated as fact, not as a report from someone else. (b) He relates with approval the story of the grammarian al-Mazini refusing, in poverty, to write out Sibawayh's book for a Jewish buyer because it contains three hundred Qur'anic verses. It is a classical anecdote about reverence for scripture, but in English it reads as a refusal to deal with a man because he is a Jew. (c) He says the Ibadis keep books which they write about others hidden away and release only to initiates. All three have been translated exactly, neither softened nor sharpened, and none has been dropped. The decision whether and how to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

This is tape fourteen of the Sheikh's course on the Islamic religious sciences (see IDs 448, 449, 450, 451, 452, 454 for other tapes). It continues the bibliographical survey begun in tape thirteen: the Shafiʿi school and its literature, the Hanbali school and its literature, and then — in what is plainly a second session joined to the first by the CMS — the Zahiri, Ibadi, Jaʿfari and Zaydi schools, and the comparative literature.

The tape is almost entirely bibliographical. Book titles are given in transliteration with diacritics and are not translated, following the practice of the other tapes in this series. Personal names follow the style guide: standard romanisation without diacritics in the body.

Technical hadith vocabulary is rendered per the glossary: 'أصح إسناد' is 'the soundest chain', 'مجهول' is 'unknown' (a narrator grading, not a general statement), 'علل' is 'hidden defects', 'يضعفها' is 'weakening them'. Where the Sheikh reports al-Bukhari's and Ibn al-Salah's judgements on the soundest chain, those attributions are kept explicit.

'أصحاب الوجوه' is rendered 'possessors of positions', the technical Shafiʿi rank, and 'الروايات المخرجة' 'the extracted reports', with the mechanism the Sheikh describes translated in full rather than summarised, since the whole point of the passage is how such reports are generated.

Where the Sheikh gives his own judgement he is marked as doing so — 'I hold that he did not breach even the Hanbali school itself except rarely', 'this is what I choose here in this sequence' — so that his voice is not confused with the survey.
The record carries no download link and is not an excerpt-only page under house rule 9; its defects are internal breaks and a joined second session, flagged individually.
